newsitem.title: UK: UK gilt market faces another year of hefty supply.
newsitem.headline: UK gilt market faces another year of hefty supply.

text.p: Britain's government bond market is bracing itself for another year of heavy supply after the Treasury announced on Wednesday that it will need to sell 36.5 billion pounds ($58 billion) of gilts in the next financial year.

With an election imminent and a change of government likely, that figure could be thrown out of the window within a couple of months, dealers said. But the amount of gilt sales required is unlikely to fall under a Labour government.
"It's a little bit on the high side, but the Treasury likes to do that so it can take some credit if it undercuts its forecast," said a senior salesman at a UK brokerage.
"And anyway you have got to take it with an enormous pinch of salt given that a new government is likely soon."

Analysts had expected total gilt sales to be no greater than 33 billion stg next year. "Perhaps it's a little on the high side but the market is not overly worried," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.

British Prime Minister John Major is expected to call an election for May 1 and with his ruling Conservative Party trailing Labour by about 20 points in the polls, the opposition party is poised to sweep to power.

Labour finance spokesman Gordon Brown has pledged to stick to Conservative spending plans for the first two years of a Labour government. But with a budget expected within weeks of a Labour victory, the government borrowing requirement could well change.

Andrew Sentance, director of the London Business School's Centre for Economic Forecasting, said public sector workers will push for hefty pay rises after years of enforced wage restraint under the Conservatives and many Labour supporters will expect more spending on education and the health service.
Despite the Labour party's attempt to distance itself from the trade unions -- its traditional allies -- it will find it hard to ignore their claims altogether.

The Treasury said a central government borrowing requirement of 20 billion pounds and 19.6 billion in gilt redemptions would be partly offset by a 3.0 billion pound contribution from National Savings in fiscal 1997/98.

Hawkins said the figures may stay broadly the same under Labour, but would not be lower. "Given their promises, if they do change anything, it is unlikely to affect the bottom line figure too much. But I don't think anyone expects issuance to be lower under a Labour government."
The salesmen said some of the changes announced by the Treasury on Wednesday were very welcome.
The government said it aims to issues more index-linked gilts -- about 20 percent of the total, up from 15 percent last year. It also hopes to start index-linked auctions.

"This year I am announcing that the authorities now see positive merits in moving to an index-linked gilts auction programme to start as soon as it is feasible," said Angela Knight, economic secretary to the Treasury.
The gilts salesman said a greater level of index-linked gilts was much in demand. "And an auction programme is long overdue as well," he said.

Hawkins said the more index-linked gilts issued, the greater the incentive for the government to keep inflation under control. Index-linked stocks, or "linkers" as they are known, pay dividends a set level above the prevailing inflation rate.
"That could be a small plus for the gilt market," he said.
And the advent of a gilt strips market, where coupons can be stripped off government bonds and traded as separate securities, would also make the market more attractive, the salesman said.
The Treasury said the gilt strips market is expected to start during the Autumn of 1997.
It intends all of next year's issues of conventional benchmark stocks will be strippable and further offers for conversion of existing unstrippable stocks are likely. ($ = 0.629 British Pounds)
